records.current_summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022 — hundreds of incidents and dozens of deaths — with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (Law 5276, the 2022 “Life and Family Protection” bill, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (a local group such as Lambda, plus trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas (Antigua, Atitlán) are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.

prison_adds.title: Every Day I Live in Fear: Violence and Discrimination Against LGBT People in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, and Obstacles to Asylum in the United States (Human Rights Watch)
prison_adds.summary: HRW (7 Oct 2020), Guatemala chapter: 'Guatemalan authorities facilitate anti-trans violence is by placing trans women in men's prisons, exposing them to violence, including sexual assault.' Bárbara Herrarte, trans activist with Redmmutrans (Red Multicultural de Mujeres Trans), described her time in a men's prison: 'Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him.' Documents birth-sex placement in the men's prison system as of 2020 with sexual-assault risk, and no gender-identity-based placement policy, special trans unit, or trans-specific solitary/segregation practice; LGBTQ org Lambda flags forced internal displacement from violence generally, but no trans-specific custody-policy or court ruling is documented in the report.

records.current_summary:
Honduras is dangerous for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the regional Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the region, outside the two largest countries.

prison_adds.title: Penitenciarias Nacionales de Honduras: una tortura para personas LGTBI - Corresponsales Clave
prison_adds.summary: Corresponsales Clave (trans activist Kendra Jordany, 6 Sep 2017), drawing on the torture-prevention centre CPTRT: trans women in Honduras' national penitentiaries are held in the MEN'S system. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the 'La Isla' module (located beside the mentally-ill unit); trans women are forced to cut their hair and barred from presenting as women ('la policia... dicen que ellas son hombres'); conjugal visits are denied. At Penitenciaria de Marcala authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after CPTRT intervention was she isolated from the men and her feminine belongings returned. Documents birth-sex placement with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad-hoc protective isolation, and no placement-by-gender-identity policy.

prison_adds.title: HRW, 'Every Day I Live in Fear': Violence and Discrimination Against LGBT People in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, and Obstacles to Asylum in the United States
prison_adds.summary: Human Rights Watch (7 Oct 2020), Honduras section: 'Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse.' A Honduran judge told HRW of a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards; the judge said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate: 'There's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.' Independent confirmation that placement operates by birth sex in the men's system, with documented sexual violence and official inaction (as of 2020).

records.current_summary:
Haiti is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the national government has effectively collapsed: gangs control most of the capital (Port-au-Prince), the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition, no protection infrastructure, and no functioning judiciary.

The trans-specific risk is inseparable from the generalised collapse — outing in gang-controlled areas can be lethal. A 2018 official US State Department report described attitudes as hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity, particularly in the capital; freshness confirms trans people remain exposed to vagrancy-law fines with zero protection or hate-crime coverage.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Haiti - Wikipedia
prison_adds.summary: Thin for the prison-housing axis: the fetched article (HTTP 200) documents Haiti's legal framework - same-sex conduct legal since 1791, no legal gender-identity recognition, no anti-discrimination protections, and a June 2017 Senate bill penalising same-sex marriage with up to three years' imprisonment - plus documented harassment of transgender people in post-earthquake camps. It contains no prison-placement practice: no birth-sex-vs-identity housing rule, no trans special units, and no solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners; no usable placement finding.

records.current_summary:
Isle of Man: a self-legislating Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea whose parliament, Tynwald, works through its own bills on these questions. The House of Keys in 2005 proactively adopted a clause protecting employees from dismissal over sexual orientation, framing it in human-rights terms; the chief minister publicly committed to marriage equality in 2015, at a time when this parliament and Northern Ireland's assembly were the only British legislatures refusing it; the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill passed its final legislative stages in April 2016 and the first civil partnership was converted to marriage that July, preserving the couple's 2015 wedding date.

Current reference material confirms the settled picture: civil partnerships from 2011, marriage since 2016, and a legal gender-recognition right in force since 2009 alongside 'gender reassignment' protections in island equality law. Claims about the metropole's single-sex code and its statutory guidance were carried in the earlier profile without primary legislative support and have been deleted, leaving the local record as the basis of this entry.

prison_adds.title: Isle of Man Prison - Wikipedia
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia article on Isle of Man Prison (Jurby), the island's only functioning prison (GBP 41.7m facility at the former RAF Jurby, fully operational 14 August 2008), operated by the Isle of Man Prison Service. Documents separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders and vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit - but no birth-sex-vs-identity placement rule, no trans special unit, and no trans-specific solitary/segregation practice; verdict thin: no usable finding on the prison-housing axis.

records.current_summary:
Ireland is a calm, comfortable destination for transgender visitors. It was one of the first countries to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration — the 2015 Gender Recognition Act lets adults change their legal gender without medical requirements — and bathroom use is unrestricted. A hate-crime law covering sexual orientation and gender identity took effect at the end of 2024, equality law bans discrimination in employment, housing and services, and marriage equality was approved by referendum in 2015.

The caveats are stagnation and a mildly worsening climate rather than active rollback. The 2015 law is binary-only and long-promised reform (non-binary, under-16s) has stalled; transphobic hate speech remains uncriminalised after a 2024 government U-turn; a university study in 2025 documented rising discrimination against sexual and gender minorities; and total hate-crime reports rose about 15% in 2025 (racism and xenophobia are the most common motives). None of this amounts to criminal exposure or physical danger for a visitor.

Day-to-day, the country is welcoming with low violent crime and a strong civil-society support network.

prison_adds.title: Guardian: Ireland's gender recognition act, a decade on (The Guardian)
prison_adds.summary: Guardian (23 Dec 2025) decade retrospective on the 2015 Gender Recognition Act: it documents the Barbie Kardashian case — a violent offender who changed name by deed poll and obtained a gender recognition certificate in 2020, then was transferred from a women's prison to a male prison during her sentence — as the case that made prison custody a focus of gender-critical campaigning in Ireland, and reports that an amendment to the GRA 'which would limit its scope so the certificate no longer changes sex for the purposes of imprisonment' has passed its first stage in the Oireachtas; the amendment was drafted by barrister Laoise de Brun (of The Countess), who cites UK gender-critical campaigners as inspiration.

prison_adds.title: Transgender history in Ireland (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia 'Transgender history in Ireland' (rev. 2 Oct 2026): documents Barbie Kardashian, a trans woman who held a Gender Recognition Certificate and a Department of Social Protection certificate recognising her as female — found guilty at Limerick Circuit Court in May 2022 of seven counts of threatening to kill or cause serious harm to her mother, and acquitted in October 2024 of separate alleged threats to a fellow prisoner and a prison officer at Limerick Prison; the article records that as of late 2025 a proposed amendment to the Gender Recognition Act 2015 that would limit the effect of a GRC 'for the purposes of imprisonment' had passed its first legislative stage, and cites the historical 1889 case of John Bradley (assigned female at birth), imprisoned at Grangegorman prison after disclosing.
